exercises.prompt: Implement getOrDefault(obj, key, fallback) so it returns obj[key] when key is actually a property of obj, and fallback when it is not. The stored value might be falsy — 0, '', or false — and those count as present, so a key that maps to 0 returns 0, not the fallback. Test membership with the in operator rather than truthiness.
hints: The trap is that obj[key] || fallback returns the fallback whenever the stored value is falsy — but a stored 0 or false should be returned as-is.
Ask whether the key is present at all, separately from its value: key in obj is true even when the value is 0, '', or false.
return key in obj ? obj[key] : fallback — read the property only once you know the key exists.

exercises.prompt: Implement sumValues(obj) so it returns the sum of all the numeric values in obj. sumValues({a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}) is 6. The keys don't matter, only the values. An empty object returns 0.
hints: You only need the values, and Object.values(obj) hands them to you as an array.
Once you have the array of values, this is the same fold you used to sum any array.
return Object.values(obj).reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0) — the 0 seed is the empty-object answer.

exercises.prompt: Implement invert(obj) so it returns a new object with keys and values swapped: each value becomes a key and its original key becomes the value. invert({a: 1, b: 2}) is {1: 'a', 2: 'b'}. Assume the values are unique strings or numbers. An empty object returns an empty object.
hints: Object.entries(obj) gives you each [key, value] pair, which is exactly what you need to flip.
Build a fresh result object and, for each pair, store result[value] = key — the old value is the new key.
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(obj)) result[value] = key, then return result — the keys of the result come from the original values.

exercises.prompt: Implement keysWhere(obj, min) so it returns an array of the keys whose value is greater than or equal to min, in the object's own key order. keysWhere({a: 1, b: 5, c: 3}, 3) is ['b', 'c']. An empty object, or one where no value reaches min, returns an empty array.
hints: Start from the keys — Object.keys(obj) — then decide which ones to keep by looking up each value.
filter keeps the keys that pass a test; the test reads the value with obj[key] and compares it to min.
return Object.keys(obj).filter(key => obj[key] >= min) — use >= so a value exactly equal to min is kept.

exercises.prompt: Implement pickDefined(obj, keys) so it returns a new object containing only the entries of obj whose key appears in the keys array AND actually exists on obj. pickDefined({a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}, ['a', 'c']) is {a: 1, c: 3}. A requested key that obj does not have is skipped. A stored value of 0 or false still counts as existing and is kept. An empty keys array, or keys none of which exist, returns an empty object.
hints: Walk the requested keys and, for each, decide whether obj really has it before copying it across.
Checking obj[key] for truthiness would drop a stored 0 or false — instead ask whether the property exists with obj.hasOwnProperty(key).
Loop the keys, and inside guard with Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key) before setting result[key] = obj[key]; return result.
